Department of Systems & Computational Biology About the School Established in 1977, The School of Life Sciences has witnessed phenomenal progress and established itself as one of the largest and most vibrant Schools in the University system in the country. With an emphasis on interdisciplinary teaching and research, the school produces finest graduates in modern biology, biotechnology, bioinformatics and systems biology. The performance of its alumni, students together with the contributions of the faculty, placed University at highest rank in research output in the recent Nature Index rankings. The School consists of five Departments: Department of Biochemistry Department of Plant Sciences Department of Animal Biology Department of Biotechnology & Bioinformatics Department of Systems & Computational Biology Every year, the School receives highest number of applications in response to our admission notifications both from India and abroad. Details of academic programmes, eligibility criteria and admission process along with faculty profile can be accessed from the web page of the school (http://sls.uohyd.ac.in). The School started its journey from a modest premises located at the old science complex. It has moved out to a new centrally air-conditioned building with a plinth area of 2,38,345 sft. The modern building is designed for housing a total of 65 research laboratories, class-rooms, teaching laboratories, central instrumentation facilities, cell and microbial culture facilities, seminar hall and auditorium. A state of the art animal house with mosquito breeding facility, and a fully functional and third party evaluated Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) facility are the recent additions to majestic School of Life Sciences building. These new additions and funding from Department of Biotechnology under DBT-Boost to University Interdisciplinary Life Science Departments for Education and Research programme (DBT-BUILDER)programme is indeed a boost to the Schools interdisciplinary research. The well-equipped laboratories, committed, trained faculty together with highly talented and motivated students contribute for establishing an excellent academic ecosystem at SLS. Under the tutelage of SLS faculty, a number of students transformed into World Class Scientists, academic leaders and entrepreneurs. Research work done by the faculty of the school frequently appear in journals of international reputes and attracted the attention of world’s best talent. resulting in establishing international collaborations. Most of the labs have won international grants and successfully participated in bilateral scientific collaborations with most of the leading nations. In recognition of their research contributions, the faculty won a number of recognitions including Millennium Plaques of Honour instituted by Indian Science Congress Association (ISCA), Shanthi Swaroop Bhatnagar Prize, given by CSIR, New Delhi. A good number of faculty are elected fellows of all three leading science academies and won coveted recognitions like JC Bose fellowships, Fulbright International Education Administrators Awards. The vision of the faculty together with hard work of the committed students, helped SLS to win institutional grants from national and international agencies. The SLS won prestigious CAS (Center for Advanced Studies) grant from University Grants Commission (UGC), New Delhi. Most of the departments of the school are funded either by UGC-DRS / by DST-FIST schemes. The SLS is one of the few Schools under University set up to receive grants from Department of Biotechnology (DBT), New Delhi under DBT-BUILDER programme. During this academic year, SLS obtained about 39 crores approximately extramural funding from both industry and Govt. funding agencies like, CSIR, DST, SERB, DBT, MoE and ICMR. Also in the country Master students of the SLS have shown impressive performance clearing UGC-CSIR-NET exam. A rigorous selection process, based on the assessment of their research writing samples by the screening committee and their reasons for enrolling in the workshop training programme, led to the selection of around 20 PhD scholars (15 from the History Department and five from Folk Culture Studies) in their third and fourth years and thesis write-up stages for these workshop sessions. In the initial phase of the three-day workshop designed for PhD scholars in Folk Culture and History, three distinguished academics with expertise in academic writing for doctoral students and the publishing industry were invited. The three resource persons who offered their insights during the three days in October were Prof. K. Satyanarayana, Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, The English and Foreign Languages University (EFLU), Hyderabad), Dr. Prasun Chatterjee Deputy Head, Primus Books, Delhi, and Dr. Hashik NK Assistant Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, Tezpur University, Assam. The three-day workshops, led by subject matter experts, were not just lecture sessions, but interactive experiences designed to engage PhD scholars. The PhD candidates specialising in Folk Culture Studies presented their ongoing research in the first phase, receiving valuable critical feedback from the resource persons who acted as evaluators during the workshop. The event primarily focused on interactive sessions, offering tips for enhancing the quality of doctoral dissertations, developing theoretical frameworks and methodologies, and ensuring that each PhD candidate contributes effectively to original research. Noteworthy sessions from the workshop included “Critical Thinking and Writing”, “Writing a Research Paper or Doctoral Thesis Chapter”, and “Transforming a Thesis into a Book Manuscript.” The second and third workshops were held on the 21st and 22nd November and 12th and 13th December, 2024. The coordinators were Professors Anindita Mukhopadhyay and Eswara Rao respectively. Due to a sudden bereavement in the family Prof. Rao could not be present during the workshop and the activities were conducted by the Head of the department. In the second phase the experts were Prof.J.Devika, Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram and Dr Pratyay Nath, Department of History, Ashoka University, Sonepat. Prof. Devika spoke on “Crafting a History of the Present of the Malayali Family: Some Thoughts” and “Towards an Intersectional Method in Writing the Histories of Subaltern Places”. Dr Pratyay Nath talked about “Methodological issues of Reading Imperial Sources against the Grain”, and “Akbar’s Pilgrimages to Ajmer and the Formation of the Mughal Empire”. He demonstrated how visual sources can be used as explanatory tools for writing history. For the third workshop our experts were Prof. Projit Behari Mukharji, Department of History, Ashoka University and Dr Meera Visvanathan, Department of Department of History, Shiv Nadar University. Projit B.Mukharji spoke on “Molecularizing Tribes: Genetics as Prosaic Science in Early Postcolonial India” and also introduced the methodology of practising History of Science, Technology and Medicine. Meera Visvanathan who is a practitioner of early Indian history, spoke on the “Complex Chronologies and Longue Durée Histories: New Narratives for Studying India’s Past” and discussed about the way a source like Land grants should be used for reconstruction of the past economic and social history. All the experts meticulously checked chapters written by the students related to their expertise and their critical comments were extremely useful. The students also presented their chapters and, in this domain, too, the experts suggested improvement which would allow them to curate their presentations in a succinct manner. The students feel that thy have hugely benefitted from the workshop, interactive sessions in particular, and the comments of the experts provided a direction to their work. The academic writing workshop emphasized the crucial skills necessary for PhD scholars aiming to become accomplished academic authors and researchers, both nationally and internationally. The resource persons and the workshop coordinator stressed the urgent necessity for PhD candidates to complete their dissertations and publish at least one peer-reviewed journal article in SCOPUS-listed journals before their PhD Viva and the awarding of their doctoral degree. The experts also emphasized on the habit of reading beyond their own research area. The workshop, in addition to offering these essential sessions, also outlined a roadmap for approaching the PhD journey as an exciting adventure filled with intellectual curiosity rather than experiencing monotony and boredom. In May 1985, the Academic Council decided that the Centre of Regional Studies would continue under the School of Social Sciences to facilitate interdisciplinary teaching and research in the field of Regional Studies, as initially recommended by the Fifth Five Year Plan Visiting Committee (AC on 15 May 1985 and EC on 13 June 1985). Established in 1985 according to the University Statutes and Ordinances, the Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) is the oldest Centre in the School of Social Sciences and the University itself. It commenced admissions for M.Phil. and Ph.D. programs from the academic year 1988-89 onwards. Since then, the Centre has awarded a total of 67 Ph.D. and 80 M.Phil. degrees from 1989-1990 to June 2024. The delineation of ‘regions’ serves as a significant framework for comprehending societal dynamics. The Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) operates as an interdisciplinary hub within the School of Social Sciences, with its focal point being the region as the unit of analysis. These regions can be further disaggregated into sub-regions, enabling a focused examination of specific themes or idiosyncrasies. These themes encompass urbanisation, industrialisation, identity conflicts, marginalised regions and groups, political intricacies, cultural underpinnings, and environmental implications. All disciplines within the realm of social sciences play pivotal roles in both the conceptualisation and implementation of this framework. CRS offers students the opportunity to engage with a regional approach to the study of socio-spatial transformations and to weave together concepts from various disciplines within the social sciences. The Centre’s educational program for students adopts a spatial perspective, providing a comprehensive understanding of complex social phenomena in their multidimensionality. This vital area of enquiry is now arousing cultural consciousness among the zealots of the exotic ranging from corporate groups to that of policy makers and social activists. The Centre for Folk Culture Studies is the first of its kind in the Central University system in India. It was established with the assistance of the Ford Foundation, USA. The Centre’s interdisciplinary and multi-perspectival approaches emphasis research and teaching in Folk Culture Studies in the milieu of contemporary ethnographic fieldwork. The Centre’s thrust is on the study of various aspects of folk expressive behaviour as a dialogue between human groups and their physical and social environments. The manifold folk forms are information banks and communication systems explicating the dynamics of adaptive processes in time and space. To decode and explain the folk expressive forms, the Centre is adopting a research strategy that combines the methodological procedures and theoretical approaches of both humanities and social sciences. The school has moved into a dedicated facility for engineering that houses several state-of-the-art laboratories under a single roof, which provides an ideal environment to pursue cross-disciplinary research in engineering sciences and technology and to effectively collaborate with other schools in the university campus. Atomic lasers, molecular computers, drug-receptor interactions, industrial catalysts, lubricants, and industrially important materials form part of this continuum and an understanding of this evolution needs all the three components of research, viz. theory, experiment and computation. Computer-based simulations now form an integral part of modern research methodology and in this era of science-driven-engineering and directed basic research, the role of scientific research, based on modelling, simulation and design, is of paramount importance. The primary requisite in using the third avenue of research for solving complex problems is a working, state-of-the- art High Performance Computing Facility (HPCF) Centre. The University of Hyderabad, having expertise in many of the above areas, fully appreciates the inter-dependence of Science, Engineering and Technology, and launched a uniquely conceived new programme of higher education and research. This initiative was launched through an imaginative programme of the UGC (recognizing the University for its Potential for excellence) by establishing a designated Centre for such activity (Centre for Modelling Simulation and Design – CMSD). This programme has been receiving generous support from DST under its FIST program. CMSD aims to nurture cross-disciplinary bridges, which are effective in generating new knowledge and creative explorations. The human resources generated from such efforts will be invaluable. Training individuals and organizations in specific hardware and software, undertaking of consultancy and turnkey projects, help convert real life phenomena into appropriate mathematical and computational models etc., are some of the important tasks that CMSD has embarked on. This Centre became operational from its new premises in December 2004. One of the unique academic features of this Centre is that all the active computational scientists working in widely different academic disciplines in the University Campus are Associate Faculty of the CMSD, and contribute their 143 50TH ANNUAL REPORT expertise and experience in furthering its academic objectives. Some of the research interests of these Members include: Physics of low dimensional systems, Topological defects in fluids in restricted geometries, Critical phenomena in complex fluids and magnetic systems, Monte Carlo simulations and development of novel sampling techniques, Genomics and bioinformatics, Protein folding, Cognitive neuroscience, Computational intelligence, Natural language understanding, Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI), Quantum Chemistry and Density Functional Theory, Molecular Modelling, Drug Design and Delivery, Design of new materials, weather forecastingetc. Short term courses have been so far conducted in the areas of Parallel Computing, Monte Carlo Simulation and Molecular Modelling etc. CMSD has been involved, over the past few years, in promoting and fostering multidisciplinary research programmes in Advanced Computational Methods, with focus on the core areas of Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Engineering Sciences and Computer Sciences, besides interest in related research areas like Finite Element Analysis as applied to Nanotechnology, Computational Fluid Dynamics, Ocean-atmosphere-climate Modelling, High-End-Visualization/ Virtual Reality, Modelling and Simulation of large/complex Systems, etc. Following are the facilities available at the Centre: 1) Data Centre: The Data Centre houses a HPC cluster with following configuration. a. The Library was established in 1975 and shifted to the present building in 1988. It was inaugurated by His Excellency Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma, the then Vice-President of India, and named after Late Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. All the in-house Library Operations are fully computerized, including the Web OPAC, using the international Library Management Software Virtua supplied by VTLS Inc., USA. The Library automation activities have been moved to the CLOUD base using AWS since 2018. The UGC-INFLIBNET has identified the Library as one of the 26 document delivery centers in India for providing photocopies of journal articles to the research scholars of other Universities. Since 1990, the Library has achieved several distinctions in the country: a) The IGM Library is the first University Library to computerize all in-house operations. b) The first Library to computerize other Libraries (B.R. Ambedkar Open University, Telangana, and State Central Library, Hyderabad, Telangana.) c) The first University Library to start the PGDLAN Course under Distance Education mode since 1998 d) The first University Library to subscribe to Electronic e-journals and databases. e) The National Board of Higher Mathematics (NBHM) has identified this Library as a Regional Library for the Southern Region. f) The first University Library to establish a Centre of competency in digital libraries and e-learning with the assistance of SUN Microsystems and UGC. g) The first University Library to install a 3M Security Gate to avoid book thefts. h) The first University Library to become a governing member of OCLC, USA. i) The first University Library to install a 100 KVA solar power system The Library is kept open 24x7 throughout the year except for Five National holidays in a year. 8.1.1. As we complete four successful years of the Institution of Eminence (IoE) project, we're poised to reach new heights. Global Recognition Our university's consistent focus on quality research and teaching has earned us a spot in the QS Rankings 2026, with a ranking of 801-850 globally. We're among the top universities worldwide and ranked 18th among Indian universities in the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) 2025. Our research publications have secured us the top spot among multidisciplinary Indian universities in the Nature Index 2025 ranking. Student Strength and Diversity This year, our student strength stands at 5,750, with 30.5% research scholars pursuing Ph.D. and M.Tech programs. Women students comprise 46.2% of the total strength, while 27.5% of students belong to reserved Basuthkar Jagadeeshwar Rao Vice-Chancellor, University of Hyderabad vii Prof. C. R. We've also seen a significant increase in international students, with 250 students enrolled in various programs. The University of Hyderabad has successfully uploaded a total of 44800 records of the Degrees awarded to the Digilocker NAD. All Degrees awarded from 1977 to 2024 have been uploaded. Our university is now part of the Ministry’s CUET for the admissions. I am happy to inform you all that the University has received close to 30,999 applications for all courses other than PhD. Research Excellence Our faculty, numbering over 400, produced more than 562 research publications including 70 books, during the year. Our faculty have been associated with several important national and international bodies, held Professorships of distinction, both in India and abroad, and participated in the global educational arena with as much vigour as we have always done. Furthermore, they have been funded quite handsomely receiving grants from national and international funding agencies like UGC, MHRD, DBT, DST, EU, DoE, IUSSTF and so on. The University’s current extramural R&D funding is about Rs. 350 crores. Our long-term vision and mission is “National Needs, Global Standards”. Our core values seek innovation and interdisciplinary, integrating hard sciences with humanistic studies and social inquiry, reinvigorating literary and linguistic studies with digital technology. University’s research work aspires to global standards in order to truly fulfil national needs. I am delighted to record here a recent study by Stanford and published in the highly respected journal PLOS Biology shows 29 of our faculty/researchers figure in the list of top researchers. Institution of Eminence Initiatives The University of Hyderabad's Institution of Eminence (IoE) status is a huge recognition of its standing and potential to join the world's best institutions. To leverage this, the university has announced several initiatives, including research calls to boost faculty research infrastructure, with 128 projects worth ₹50 crores already awarded. The latest research call focuses on SC/ST/Women and persons with disability. The university is also working on internationalization through the IoE Chair Professor and International Fellows scheme, and enhancing industry involvement through public-private partnerships and research clusters. New infrastructure developments are Inter-disciplinary centre; HRDC building; International guest house; Administrative building and Hostels for boys and girls. NEP 2020 and IoE Initiatives We're committed to implementing the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, focusing on interdisciplinary research, innovation, and community engagement. Under the IoE project, we've launched new programs, viii ix including research calls, professional development funds for teachers, and student achiever awards. We've also initiated internationalization efforts, including the IoE Chair Professor and International Fellows scheme. Infrastructure Development We're expanding our infrastructure with new buildings, including an interdisciplinary center, HRDC building, international guest house, and hostels. These developments will enhance our research and teaching capabilities. Looking Ahead As we strive to become a global leader in higher education, our vision of "National Needs, Global Standards" aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). I congratulate our faculty, students, and staff for their tireless efforts and dedication to excellence. I look forward to even greater achievements for the University of Hyderabad. Department of Systems & Computational Biology About the School Established in 1977, The School of Life Sciences has witnessed phenomenal progress and established itself as one of the largest and most vibrant Schools in the University system in the country. With an emphasis on interdisciplinary teaching and research, the school produces finest graduates in modern biology, biotechnology, bioinformatics and systems biology. The performance of its alumni, students together with the contributions of the faculty, placed University at highest rank in research output in the recent Nature Index rankings. The School consists of five Departments: Department of Biochemistry Department of Plant Sciences Department of Animal Biology Department of Biotechnology & Bioinformatics Department of Systems & Computational Biology Every year, the School receives highest number of applications in response to our admission notifications both from India and abroad. Details of academic programmes, eligibility criteria and admission process along with faculty profile can be accessed from the web page of the school (http://sls.uohyd.ac.in). The School started its journey from a modest premises located at the old science complex. It has moved out to a new centrally air-conditioned building with a plinth area of 2,38,345 sft. The modern building is designed for housing a total of 65 research laboratories, class-rooms, teaching laboratories, central instrumentation facilities, cell and microbial culture facilities, seminar hall and auditorium. A state of the art animal house with mosquito breeding facility, and a fully functional and third party evaluated Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) facility are the recent additions to majestic School of Life Sciences building. These new additions and funding from Department of Biotechnology under DBT-Boost to University Interdisciplinary Life Science Departments for Education and Research programme (DBT-BUILDER)programme is indeed a boost to the Schools interdisciplinary research. Under the tutelage of SLS faculty, a number of students transformed into World Class Scientists, academic leaders and entrepreneurs. Most of the labs have won international grants and successfully participated in bilateral scientific collaborations with most of the leading nations. A rigorous selection process, based on the assessment of their research writing samples by the screening committee and their reasons for enrolling in the workshop training programme, led to the selection of around 20 PhD scholars (15 from the History Department and five from Folk Culture Studies) in their third and fourth years and thesis write-up stages for these workshop sessions. In the initial phase of the three-day workshop designed for PhD scholars in Folk Culture and History, three distinguished academics with expertise in academic writing for doctoral students and the publishing industry were invited. The three resource persons who offered their insights during the three days in October were Prof. K. Satyanarayana, Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, The English and Foreign Languages University (EFLU), Hyderabad), Dr. Prasun Chatterjee Deputy Head, Primus Books, Delhi, and Dr. Hashik NK Assistant Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, Tezpur University, Assam. The three-day workshops, led by subject matter experts, were not just lecture sessions, but interactive experiences designed to engage PhD scholars. The PhD candidates specialising in Folk Culture Studies presented their ongoing research in the first phase, receiving valuable critical feedback from the resource persons who acted as evaluators during the workshop. The event primarily focused on interactive sessions, offering tips for enhancing the quality of doctoral dissertations, developing theoretical frameworks and methodologies, and ensuring that each PhD candidate contributes effectively to original research. Noteworthy sessions from the workshop included “Critical Thinking and Writing”, “Writing a Research Paper or Doctoral Thesis Chapter”, and “Transforming a Thesis into a Book Manuscript.” The second and third workshops were held on the 21st and 22nd November and 12th and 13th December, 2024. The coordinators were Professors Anindita Mukhopadhyay and Eswara Rao respectively. Due to a sudden bereavement in the family Prof. Rao could not be present during the workshop and the activities were conducted by the Head of the department. In the second phase the experts were Prof.J.Devika, Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram and Dr Pratyay Nath, Department of History, Ashoka University, Sonepat. Prof. Devika spoke on “Crafting a History of the Present of the Malayali Family: Some Thoughts” and “Towards an Intersectional Method in Writing the Histories of Subaltern Places”. Dr Pratyay Nath talked about “Methodological issues of Reading Imperial Sources against the Grain”, and “Akbar’s Pilgrimages to Ajmer and the Formation of the Mughal Empire”. He demonstrated how visual sources can be used as explanatory tools for writing history. For the third workshop our experts were Prof. Projit Behari Mukharji, Department of History, Ashoka University and Dr Meera Visvanathan, Department of Department of History, Shiv Nadar University. Projit B.Mukharji spoke on “Molecularizing Tribes: Genetics as Prosaic Science in Early Postcolonial India” and also introduced the methodology of practising History of Science, Technology and Medicine. Meera Visvanathan who is a practitioner of early Indian history, spoke on the “Complex Chronologies and Longue Durée Histories: New Narratives for Studying India’s Past” and discussed about the way a source like Land grants should be used for reconstruction of the past economic and social history. All the experts meticulously checked chapters written by the students related to their expertise and their critical comments were extremely useful. The students also presented their chapters and, in this domain, too, the experts suggested improvement which would allow them to curate their presentations in a succinct manner. The students feel that thy have hugely benefitted from the workshop, interactive sessions in particular, and the comments of the experts provided a direction to their work. The academic writing workshop emphasized the crucial skills necessary for PhD scholars aiming to become accomplished academic authors and researchers, both nationally and internationally. The resource persons and the workshop coordinator stressed the urgent necessity for PhD candidates to complete their dissertations and publish at least one peer-reviewed journal article in SCOPUS-listed journals before their PhD Viva and the awarding of their doctoral degree. The experts also emphasized on the habit of reading beyond their own research area. The workshop, in addition to offering these essential sessions, also outlined a roadmap for approaching the PhD journey as an exciting adventure filled with intellectual curiosity rather than experiencing monotony and boredom. In May 1985, the Academic Council decided that the Centre of Regional Studies would continue under the School of Social Sciences to facilitate interdisciplinary teaching and research in the field of Regional Studies, as initially recommended by the Fifth Five Year Plan Visiting Committee (AC on 15 May 1985 and EC on 13 June 1985). Established in 1985 according to the University Statutes and Ordinances, the Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) is the oldest Centre in the School of Social Sciences and the University itself. It commenced admissions for M.Phil. and Ph.D. programs from the academic year 1988-89 onwards. Since then, the Centre has awarded a total of 67 Ph.D. and 80 M.Phil. degrees from 1989-1990 to June 2024. The delineation of ‘regions’ serves as a significant framework for comprehending societal dynamics. The Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) operates as an interdisciplinary hub within the School of Social Sciences, with its focal point being the region as the unit of analysis. These regions can be further disaggregated into sub-regions, enabling a focused examination of specific themes or idiosyncrasies. These themes encompass urbanisation, industrialisation, identity conflicts, marginalised regions and groups, political intricacies, cultural underpinnings, and environmental implications. All disciplines within the realm of social sciences play pivotal roles in both the conceptualisation and implementation of this framework. CRS offers students the opportunity to engage with a regional approach to the study of socio-spatial transformations and to weave together concepts from various disciplines within the social sciences. The Centre’s educational program for students adopts a spatial perspective, providing a comprehensive understanding of complex social phenomena in their multidimensionality. This vital area of enquiry is now arousing cultural consciousness among the zealots of the exotic ranging from corporate groups to that of policy makers and social activists. The Centre for Folk Culture Studies is the first of its kind in the Central University system in India. It was established with the assistance of the Ford Foundation, USA. The Centre’s interdisciplinary and multi-perspectival approaches emphasis research and teaching in Folk Culture Studies in the milieu of contemporary ethnographic fieldwork. The Centre’s thrust is on the study of various aspects of folk expressive behaviour as a dialogue between human groups and their physical and social environments. The manifold folk forms are information banks and communication systems explicating the dynamics of adaptive processes in time and space. To decode and explain the folk expressive forms, the Centre is adopting a research strategy that combines the methodological procedures and theoretical approaches of both humanities and social sciences. At present, SEST offers M.Tech programmes in Materials Engineering, Nanoscience and Technology and Manufacturing Science and Engineering and Ph.D. programmes in Materials Engineering and Nanoscience and Technology and intends to offer Ph.D. programme in Manufacturing Science and Engineering soon. The school will be starting an integrated 5-year B.Tech & M.Tech program in Materials engineering from the academic year 2024. With this addition, the school will seamlessly cater to engineering 135 50TH ANNUAL REPORT education from the bachelor’s level to doctoral level. Furthermore, the school plans to offer new programs in emerging areas of engineering and specialized programs for working professionals. The school has moved into a dedicated facility for engineering that houses several state-of-the-art laboratories under a single roof, which provides an ideal environment to pursue cross-disciplinary research in engineering sciences and technology and to effectively collaborate with other schools in the university campus. Atomic lasers, molecular computers, drug-receptor interactions, industrial catalysts, lubricants, and industrially important materials form part of this continuum and an understanding of this evolution needs all the three components of research, viz. theory, experiment and computation. Computer-based simulations now form an integral part of modern research methodology and in this era of science-driven-engineering and directed basic research, the role of scientific research, based on modelling, simulation and design, is of paramount importance. The primary requisite in using the third avenue of research for solving complex problems is a working, state-of-the- art High Performance Computing Facility (HPCF) Centre. The University of Hyderabad, having expertise in many of the above areas, fully appreciates the inter-dependence of Science, Engineering and Technology, and launched a uniquely conceived new programme of higher education and research. This initiative was launched through an imaginative programme of the UGC (recognizing the University for its Potential for excellence) by establishing a designated Centre for such activity (Centre for Modelling Simulation and Design – CMSD). This programme has been receiving generous support from DST under its FIST program. CMSD aims to nurture cross-disciplinary bridges, which are effective in generating new knowledge and creative explorations. The human resources generated from such efforts will be invaluable. Training individuals and organizations in specific hardware and software, undertaking of consultancy and turnkey projects, help convert real life phenomena into appropriate mathematical and computational models etc., are some of the important tasks that CMSD has embarked on. This Centre became operational from its new premises in December 2004. One of the unique academic features of this Centre is that all the active computational scientists working in widely different academic disciplines in the University Campus are Associate Faculty of the CMSD, and contribute their 143 50TH ANNUAL REPORT expertise and experience in furthering its academic objectives. Some of the research interests of these Members include: Physics of low dimensional systems, Topological defects in fluids in restricted geometries, Critical phenomena in complex fluids and magnetic systems, Monte Carlo simulations and development of novel sampling techniques, Genomics and bioinformatics, Protein folding, Cognitive neuroscience, Computational intelligence, Natural language understanding, Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI), Quantum Chemistry and Density Functional Theory, Molecular Modelling, Drug Design and Delivery, Design of new materials, weather forecastingetc. Short term courses have been so far conducted in the areas of Parallel Computing, Monte Carlo Simulation and Molecular Modelling etc. CMSD has been involved, over the past few years, in promoting and fostering multidisciplinary research programmes in Advanced Computational Methods, with focus on the core areas of Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Engineering Sciences and Computer Sciences, besides interest in related research areas like Finite Element Analysis as applied to Nanotechnology, Computational Fluid Dynamics, Ocean-atmosphere-climate Modelling, High-End-Visualization/ Virtual Reality, Modelling and Simulation of large/complex Systems, etc. Following are the facilities available at the Centre: 1) Data Centre: The Data Centre houses a HPC cluster with following configuration. a. Institution of Eminence (IoE): The Government of India accorded the Institution of Eminence (IoE) status to University of Hyderabad in September 2019, in recognition of its standing, ability and potential to move into the league of the world’s best institutions. Only two other Central universities, Banaras Hindu University and University of Delhi have been accorded this status. University of Hyderabad is the only Central University in South India to achieve this status. The IoE tagline ‘national needs, global standards’ is geared towards academic, research, infrastructure, financial and administrative support for all its stakeholders: faculty, students and non-teaching staff. The university views IoE as a unique opportunity in its history to leverage its existing reputation, practices and services to catapult itself into the best and highest leagues nationally and globally. The University has spent more than ₹600 crore so far on achieving the IoE goals. A substantial part of IoE funds have been invested in creation of new infrastructure including upgrading of existing equipment and research support; a new Interdisciplinary Research Centre to house central facilities, enable conferences and innovation and entrepreneurship; human resource development centre; 50 room guest house, 400-seater boys and girls’ hostel (each); lecture hall complex; and administration building. Most of these buildings are either complete and ready for occupation or very close to completion. The central facilities being established at a cost of ₹60 crore include an analytical Transmission Electron microscope, focused ion beam- scanning electron microscope, micro-x-ray diffractometer, x-ray photoelectron spectrometer, optical microscopy platforms, physical property measurement system etc. More than 250 faculty members out of the total faculty strength of 400 have been awarded grants through the five research calls and professional development fund schemes. Uniquely, one of the research calls was aimed at funding the research programmes of faculty members belonging to the SC/ST/Women/PwD categories. Two other schemes aimed at encouraging translational research and greater engagement with the industry called inter-institutional research clusters and public-private partnerships were also launched. This initiative is helping in facilitating exposure of UoH faculty to their international counterparts and industry. A research cluster on the applications of AI in the health sector has been established. 167 50TH ANNUAL REPORT Almost 500 faculty members and PhD scholars have received the ₹1 lakh travel assistance to attend seminars and conferences abroad. In addition, over the last two years, close to 150 non-NET PhD scholars have received the publication-based performance incentive of ₹ 12,000/- per month. More than 200 PG students have received the cash award of ₹ 5,000 for being the topper in a semester in a PG programme along with a certificate. About 75 post-doctoral research fellows have also been appointed under the IoE programme. The IoE programme has funded more than 100 national and international conferences cutting across disciplines, short- term visits of 5 internationally eminent IoE-Chair Professors, several skill development programmes and development of e-learning resources. Global Recognition Our university's consistent focus on quality research and teaching has earned us a spot in the QS Rankings 2026, with a ranking of 801-850 globally. Our research publications have secured us the top spot among multidisciplinary Indian universities in the Nature Index 2025 ranking. Research Excellence Our faculty, numbering over 400, produced more than 562 research publications including 70 books, during the year. Our faculty have been associated with several important national and international bodies, held Professorships of distinction, both in India and abroad, and participated in the global educational arena with as much vigour as we have always done. Furthermore, they have been funded quite handsomely receiving grants from national and international funding agencies like UGC, MHRD, DBT, DST, EU, DoE, IUSSTF and so on. The University’s current extramural R&D funding is about Rs. 350 crores. Our long-term vision and mission is “National Needs, Global Standards”. Our core values seek innovation and interdisciplinary, integrating hard sciences with humanistic studies and social inquiry, reinvigorating literary and linguistic studies with digital technology. University’s research work aspires to global standards in order to truly fulfil national needs. I am delighted to record here a recent study by Stanford and published in the highly respected journal PLOS Biology shows 29 of our faculty/researchers figure in the list of top researchers. Institution of Eminence Initiatives The University of Hyderabad's Institution of Eminence (IoE) status is a huge recognition of its standing and potential to join the world's best institutions. To leverage this, the university has announced several initiatives, including research calls to boost faculty research infrastructure, with 128 projects worth ₹50 crores already awarded. The latest research call focuses on SC/ST/Women and persons with disability. The university is also working on internationalization through the IoE Chair Professor and International Fellows scheme, and enhancing industry involvement through public-private partnerships and research clusters. New infrastructure developments are Inter-disciplinary centre; HRDC building; International guest house; Administrative building and Hostels for boys and girls. NEP 2020 and IoE Initiatives We're committed to implementing the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, focusing on interdisciplinary research, innovation, and community engagement. Under the IoE project, we've launched new programs, viii ix including research calls, professional development funds for teachers, and student achiever awards. We've also initiated internationalization efforts, including the IoE Chair Professor and International Fellows scheme. Infrastructure Development We're expanding our infrastructure with new buildings, including an interdisciplinary center, HRDC building, international guest house, and hostels. These developments will enhance our research and teaching capabilities. Looking Ahead As we strive to become a global leader in higher education, our vision of "National Needs, Global Standards" aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). I congratulate our faculty, students, and staff for their tireless efforts and dedication to excellence. I look forward to even greater achievements for the University of Hyderabad. Department of Systems & Computational Biology About the School Established in 1977, The School of Life Sciences has witnessed phenomenal progress and established itself as one of the largest and most vibrant Schools in the University system in the country. With an emphasis on interdisciplinary teaching and research, the school produces finest graduates in modern biology, biotechnology, bioinformatics and systems biology. The performance of its alumni, students together with the contributions of the faculty, placed University at highest rank in research output in the recent Nature Index rankings. The School consists of five Departments: Department of Biochemistry Department of Plant Sciences Department of Animal Biology Department of Biotechnology & Bioinformatics Department of Systems & Computational Biology Every year, the School receives highest number of applications in response to our admission notifications both from India and abroad. Details of academic programmes, eligibility criteria and admission process along with faculty profile can be accessed from the web page of the school (http://sls.uohyd.ac.in). The School started its journey from a modest premises located at the old science complex. It has moved out to a new centrally air-conditioned building with a plinth area of 2,38,345 sft. The modern building is designed for housing a total of 65 research laboratories, class-rooms, teaching laboratories, central instrumentation facilities, cell and microbial culture facilities, seminar hall and auditorium. A state of the art animal house with mosquito breeding facility, and a fully functional and third party evaluated Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) facility are the recent additions to majestic School of Life Sciences building. These new additions and funding from Department of Biotechnology under DBT-Boost to University Interdisciplinary Life Science Departments for Education and Research programme (DBT-BUILDER)programme is indeed a boost to the Schools interdisciplinary research. The well-equipped laboratories, committed, trained faculty together with highly talented and motivated students contribute for establishing an excellent academic ecosystem at SLS. Under the tutelage of SLS faculty, a number of students transformed into World Class Scientists, academic leaders and entrepreneurs. Research work done by the faculty of the school frequently appear in journals of international reputes and attracted the attention of world’s best talent. resulting in establishing international collaborations. Most of the labs have won international grants and successfully participated in bilateral scientific collaborations with most of the leading nations. In recognition of their research contributions, the faculty won a number of recognitions including Millennium Plaques of Honour instituted by Indian Science Congress Association (ISCA), Shanthi Swaroop Bhatnagar Prize, given by CSIR, New Delhi. A good number of faculty are elected fellows of all three leading science academies and won coveted recognitions like JC Bose fellowships, Fulbright International Education Administrators Awards. The vision of the faculty together with hard work of the committed students, helped SLS to win institutional grants from national and international agencies. The SLS won prestigious CAS (Center for Advanced Studies) grant from University Grants Commission (UGC), New Delhi. Most of the departments of the school are funded either by UGC-DRS / by DST-FIST schemes. The SLS is one of the few Schools under University set up to receive grants from Department of Biotechnology (DBT), New Delhi under DBT-BUILDER programme. A rigorous selection process, based on the assessment of their research writing samples by the screening committee and their reasons for enrolling in the workshop training programme, led to the selection of around 20 PhD scholars (15 from the History Department and five from Folk Culture Studies) in their third and fourth years and thesis write-up stages for these workshop sessions. In the initial phase of the three-day workshop designed for PhD scholars in Folk Culture and History, three distinguished academics with expertise in academic writing for doctoral students and the publishing industry were invited. The three resource persons who offered their insights during the three days in October were Prof. K. Satyanarayana, Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, The English and Foreign Languages University (EFLU), Hyderabad), Dr. Prasun Chatterjee Deputy Head, Primus Books, Delhi, and Dr. Hashik NK Assistant Professor, Department of Cultural Studies, Tezpur University, Assam. The three-day workshops, led by subject matter experts, were not just lecture sessions, but interactive experiences designed to engage PhD scholars. The PhD candidates specialising in Folk Culture Studies presented their ongoing research in the first phase, receiving valuable critical feedback from the resource persons who acted as evaluators during the workshop. The event primarily focused on interactive sessions, offering tips for enhancing the quality of doctoral dissertations, developing theoretical frameworks and methodologies, and ensuring that each PhD candidate contributes effectively to original research. Noteworthy sessions from the workshop included “Critical Thinking and Writing”, “Writing a Research Paper or Doctoral Thesis Chapter”, and “Transforming a Thesis into a Book Manuscript.” The second and third workshops were held on the 21st and 22nd November and 12th and 13th December, 2024. The coordinators were Professors Anindita Mukhopadhyay and Eswara Rao respectively. In May 1985, the Academic Council decided that the Centre of Regional Studies would continue under the School of Social Sciences to facilitate interdisciplinary teaching and research in the field of Regional Studies, as initially recommended by the Fifth Five Year Plan Visiting Committee (AC on 15 May 1985 and EC on 13 June 1985). Established in 1985 according to the University Statutes and Ordinances, the Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) is the oldest Centre in the School of Social Sciences and the University itself. It commenced admissions for M.Phil. and Ph.D. programs from the academic year 1988-89 onwards. Since then, the Centre has awarded a total of 67 Ph.D. and 80 M.Phil. degrees from 1989-1990 to June 2024. The delineation of ‘regions’ serves as a significant framework for comprehending societal dynamics. The Centre for Regional Studies (CRS) operates as an interdisciplinary hub within the School of Social Sciences, with its focal point being the region as the unit of analysis. These regions can be further disaggregated into sub-regions, enabling a focused examination of specific themes or idiosyncrasies. These themes encompass urbanisation, industrialisation, identity conflicts, marginalised regions and groups, political intricacies, cultural underpinnings, and environmental implications. All disciplines within the realm of social sciences play pivotal roles in both the conceptualisation and implementation of this framework. CRS offers students the opportunity to engage with a regional approach to the study of socio-spatial transformations and to weave together concepts from various disciplines within the social sciences. The Centre’s educational program for students adopts a spatial perspective, providing a comprehensive understanding of complex social phenomena in their multidimensionality. The Centre for Folk Culture Studies is the first of its kind in the Central University system in India. It was established with the assistance of the Ford Foundation, USA. The Centre’s interdisciplinary and multi-perspectival approaches emphasis research and teaching in Folk Culture Studies in the milieu of contemporary ethnographic fieldwork. The Centre’s thrust is on the study of various aspects of folk expressive behaviour as a dialogue between human groups and their physical and social environments. The manifold folk forms are information banks and communication systems explicating the dynamics of adaptive processes in time and space. To decode and explain the folk expressive forms, the Centre is adopting a research strategy that combines the methodological procedures and theoretical approaches of both humanities and social sciences. As one of the core departments of the Sarojini Naidu School of Arts & Communication, the department remains committed to advancing contemporary art practice, strengthening interdisciplinary learning, and nurturing the next generation of artists, researchers, and educators. The academic year witnessed a rich spectrum of events including exhibitions, workshops, visiting artist lectures, community-based projects, and student-led initiatives. Faculty members actively contributed to national and international art discourse through exhibitions, publications, invited talks, and academic engagements. Students of Painting, Printmaking, and Sculpture demonstrated strong participation in exhibitions, scholarships, studio practice, internships, and community projects. Aligned with the University’s mission and the Institution of Eminence mandate, the department continued upgrading its studios, enhancing pedagogic processes, and strengthening research orientation in practice- based and theory-based domains. The year also marked collaborations with art institutions, galleries, and cultural organizations, expanding visibility and institutional outreach. Atomic lasers, molecular computers, drug-receptor interactions, industrial catalysts, lubricants, and industrially important materials form part of this continuum and an understanding of this evolution needs all the three components of research, viz. theory, experiment and computation. Computer-based simulations now form an integral part of modern research methodology and in this era of science-driven-engineering and directed basic research, the role of scientific research, based on modelling, simulation and design, is of paramount importance. The primary requisite in using the third avenue of research for solving complex problems is a working, state-of-the- art High Performance Computing Facility (HPCF) Centre. The University of Hyderabad, having expertise in many of the above areas, fully appreciates the inter-dependence of Science, Engineering and Technology, and launched a uniquely conceived new programme of higher education and research. This initiative was launched through an imaginative programme of the UGC (recognizing the University for its Potential for excellence) by establishing a designated Centre for such activity (Centre for Modelling Simulation and Design – CMSD). This programme has been receiving generous support from DST under its FIST program. CMSD aims to nurture cross-disciplinary bridges, which are effective in generating new knowledge and creative explorations. The human resources generated from such efforts will be invaluable. Training individuals and organizations in specific hardware and software, undertaking of consultancy and turnkey projects, help convert real life phenomena into appropriate mathematical and computational models etc., are some of the important tasks that CMSD has embarked on. This Centre became operational from its new premises in December 2004. CHAPTER 1 158 CHAPTER 8 Chapter 8 Central Facilities 8.1 Indira Gandhi Memorial Library The Indira Gandhi Memorial Library is a central facility that provides information and support for the University’s academic and research activities. The Library was established in 1975 and shifted to the present building in 1988. It was inaugurated by His Excellency Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma, the then Vice-President of India, and named after Late Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. All the in-house Library Operations are fully computerized, including the Web OPAC, using the international Library Management Software Virtua supplied by VTLS Inc., USA. The Library automation activities have been moved to the CLOUD base using AWS since 2018. The UGC-INFLIBNET has identified the Library as one of the 26 document delivery centers in India for providing photocopies of journal articles to the research scholars of other Universities. Since 1990, the Library has achieved several distinctions in the country: a) The IGM Library is the first University Library to computerize all in-house operations. b) The first Library to computerize other Libraries (B.R. Ambedkar Open University, Telangana, and State Central Library, Hyderabad, Telangana.) c) The first University Library to start the PGDLAN Course under Distance Education mode since 1998 d) The first University Library to subscribe to Electronic e-journals and databases. e) The National Board of Higher Mathematics (NBHM) has identified this Library as a Regional Library for the Southern Region. f) The first University Library to establish a Centre of competency in digital libraries and e-learning with the assistance of SUN Microsystems and UGC. g) The first University Library to install a 3M Security Gate to avoid book thefts. h) The first University Library to become a governing member of OCLC, USA. i) The first University Library to install a 100 KVA solar power system The Library is kept open 24x7 throughout the year except for Five National holidays in a year. 8.1.1. Institution of Eminence (IoE): The Government of India accorded the Institution of Eminence (IoE) status to University of Hyderabad in September 2019, in recognition of its standing, ability and potential to move into the league of the world’s best institutions. Only two other Central universities, Banaras Hindu University and University of Delhi have been accorded this status. University of Hyderabad is the only Central University in South India to achieve this status. The IoE tagline ‘national needs, global standards’ is geared towards academic, research, infrastructure, financial and administrative support for all its stakeholders: faculty, students and non-teaching staff. The university views IoE as a unique opportunity in its history to leverage its existing reputation, practices and services to catapult itself into the best and highest leagues nationally and globally. The University has spent more than ₹600 crore so far on achieving the IoE goals. A substantial part of IoE funds have been invested in creation of new infrastructure including upgrading of existing equipment and research support; a new Interdisciplinary Research Centre to house central facilities, enable conferences and innovation and entrepreneurship; human resource development centre; 50 room guest house, 400-seater boys and girls’ hostel (each); lecture hall complex; and administration building. Most of these buildings are either complete and ready for occupation or very close to completion. The central facilities being established at a cost of ₹60 crore include an analytical Transmission Electron microscope, focused ion beam- scanning electron microscope, micro-x-ray diffractometer, x-ray photoelectron spectrometer, optical microscopy platforms, physical property measurement system etc. More than 250 faculty members out of the total faculty strength of 400 have been awarded grants through the five research calls and professional development fund schemes. Uniquely, one of the research calls was aimed at funding the research programmes of faculty members belonging to the SC/ST/Women/PwD categories. Two other schemes aimed at encouraging translational research and greater engagement with the industry called inter-institutional research clusters and public-private partnerships were also launched. A research cluster on the applications of AI in the health sector has been established. 167 50TH ANNUAL REPORT Almost 500 faculty members and PhD scholars have received the ₹1 lakh travel assistance to attend seminars and conferences abroad. department of history, in collaboration with the centre for folk culture studies—part of the institute of eminence and the school of social sciences at the university of hyderabad—organised the golden jubilee academic writing workshops in october, november, and december 2024 under the auspices of the school of social sciences. 109 50th annual report dr vijay ramdas mandala coordinated the first phase of a three-day academic writing workshop held on 21st, 22nd, and 23rd october 2024 at the conference hall, school of social sciences in the university of hyderabad. a rigorous selection process, based on the assessment of their research writing samples by the screening committee and their reasons for enrolling in the workshop training programme, led to the selection of around 20 phd scholars (15 from the history department and five from folk culture studies) in their third and fourth years and thesis write-up stages for these workshop sessions. in the initial phase of the three-day workshop designed for phd scholars in folk culture and history, three distinguished academics with expertise in academic writing for doctoral students and the publishing industry were invited. the three resource persons who offered their insights during the three days in october were prof. k. satyanarayana, professor, department of cultural studies, the english and foreign languages university (eflu), hyderabad), dr. prasun chatterjee deputy head, primus books, delhi, and dr. hashik nk assistant professor, department of cultural studies, tezpur university, assam. the three-day workshops, led by subject matter experts, were not just lecture sessions, but interactive experiences designed to engage phd scholars. the phd candidates specialising in folk culture studies presented their ongoing research in the first phase, receiving valuable critical feedback from the resource persons who acted as evaluators during the workshop. the event primarily focused on interactive sessions, offering tips for enhancing the quality of doctoral dissertations, developing theoretical frameworks and methodologies, and ensuring that each phd candidate contributes effectively to original research. noteworthy sessions from the workshop included “critical thinking and writing”, “writing a research paper or doctoral thesis chapter”, and “transforming a thesis into a book manuscript.” the second and third workshops were held on the 21st and 22nd november and 12th and 13th december, 2024. the coordinators were professors anindita mukhopadhyay and eswara rao respectively. due to a sudden bereavement in the family prof. rao could not be present during the workshop and the activities were conducted by the head of the department. in the second phase the experts were prof.j.devika, centre for development studies, thiruvananthapuram and dr pratyay nath, department of history, ashoka university, sonepat. prof. devika spoke on “crafting a history of the present of the malayali family: some thoughts” and “towards an intersectional method in writing the histories of subaltern places”. dr pratyay nath talked about “methodological issues of reading imperial sources against the grain”, and “akbar’s pilgrimages to ajmer and the formation of the mughal empire”. he demonstrated how visual sources can be used as explanatory tools for writing history. for the third workshop our experts were prof. projit behari mukharji, department of history, ashoka university and dr meera visvanathan, department of department of history, shiv nadar university. projit b.mukharji spoke on “molecularizing tribes: genetics as prosaic science in early postcolonial india” and also introduced the methodology of practising history of science, technology and medicine. meera visvanathan who is a practitioner of early indian history, spoke on the “complex chronologies and longue durée histories: new narratives for studying india’s past” and discussed about the way a source like land grants should be used for reconstruction of the past economic and social history. all the experts meticulously checked chapters written by the students related to their expertise and their critical comments were extremely useful. the students also presented their chapters and, in this domain, too, the experts suggested improvement which would allow them to curate their presentations in a succinct manner. the students feel that thy have hugely benefitted from the workshop, interactive sessions in particular, and the comments of the experts provided a direction to their work. the academic writing workshop emphasized the crucial skills necessary for phd scholars aiming to become accomplished academic authors and researchers, both nationally and internationally. the resource persons and the workshop coordinator stressed the urgent necessity for phd candidates to complete their dissertations and publish at least one peer-reviewed journal article in scopus-listed journals before their phd viva and the awarding of their doctoral degree. the experts also emphasized on the habit of reading beyond their own research area. the workshop, in addition to offering these essential sessions, also outlined a roadmap for approaching the phd journey as an exciting adventure filled with intellectual curiosity rather than experiencing monotony and boredom. number of seminars / conferences university on 4 april 1977. in may 1985, the academic council decided that the centre of regional studies would continue under the school of social sciences to facilitate interdisciplinary teaching and research in the field of regional studies, as initially recommended by the fifth five year plan visiting committee (ac on 15 may 1985 and ec on 13 june 1985). established in 1985 according to the university statutes and ordinances, the centre for regional studies (crs) is the oldest centre in the school of social sciences and the university itself. it commenced admissions for m.phil. and ph.d. programs from the academic year 1988-89 onwards. since then, the centre has awarded a total of 67 ph.d. and 80 m.phil. degrees from 1989-1990 to june 2024. the delineation of ‘regions’ serves as a significant framework for comprehending societal dynamics. the centre for regional studies (crs) operates as an interdisciplinary hub within the school of social sciences, with its focal point being the region as the unit of analysis. these regions can be further disaggregated into sub-regions, enabling a focused examination of specific themes or idiosyncrasies. these themes encompass urbanisation, industrialisation, identity conflicts, marginalised regions and groups, political intricacies, cultural underpinnings, and environmental implications. all disciplines within the realm of social sciences play pivotal roles in both the conceptualisation and implementation of this framework. crs offers students the opportunity to engage with a regional approach to the study of socio-spatial transformations and to weave together concepts from various disciplines within the social sciences. the centre’s educational program for students adopts a spatial perspective, providing a comprehensive understanding of complex social phenomena in their multidimensionality. head of the centre : prof. v. srinivasa rao faculty as per seniority professors : dr. v. srinivasa rao associate culture studies faculty list according to seniority: in the wake of globalization, indian culture in general and folk culture in particular needs special attention to safeguard its own identity and heritage. this vital area of enquiry is now arousing cultural consciousness among the zealots of the exotic ranging from corporate groups to that of policy makers and social activists. the centre for folk culture studies is the first of its kind in the central university system in india. it was established with the assistance of the ford foundation, usa. the centre’s interdisciplinary and multi-perspectival approaches emphasis research and teaching in folk culture studies in the milieu of contemporary ethnographic fieldwork. the centre’s thrust is on the study of various aspects of folk expressive behaviour as a dialogue between human groups and their physical and social environments. the manifold folk forms are information banks and communication systems explicating the dynamics of adaptive processes in time and space. to decode and explain the folk expressive forms, the centre is adopting a research strategy that combines the methodological procedures and theoretical approaches of both humanities and social sciences. apart from the nep electives, gec and optional courses, the centre is offering ph. d programme and the current strength is nine. of atoms and molecules to the macro world of solids, liquid and gases calls for an understanding of a variety of phenomena in physics, chemistry, biology, technology and related areas. atomic lasers, molecular computers, drug-receptor interactions, industrial catalysts, lubricants, and industrially important materials form part of this continuum and an understanding of this evolution needs all the three components of research, viz. theory, experiment and computation. computer-based simulations now form an integral part of modern research methodology and in this era of science-driven-engineering and directed basic research, the role of scientific research, based on modelling, simulation and design, is of paramount importance. the primary requisite in using the third avenue of research for solving complex problems is a working, state-of-the- art high performance computing facility (hpcf) centre. the university of hyderabad, having expertise in many of the above areas, fully appreciates the inter-dependence of science, engineering and technology, and launched a uniquely conceived new programme of higher education and research. this initiative was launched through an imaginative programme of the ugc (recognizing the university for its potential for excellence) by establishing a designated centre for such activity (centre for modelling simulation and design – cmsd). this programme has been receiving generous support from dst under its fist program. cmsd aims to nurture cross-disciplinary bridges, which are effective in generating new knowledge and creative explorations. the human resources generated from such efforts will be invaluable. training individuals and organizations in specific hardware and software, undertaking of consultancy and turnkey projects, help convert real life phenomena into appropriate mathematical and computational models etc., are some of the important tasks that cmsd has embarked on. this centre became operational from notice_text: Page 1 of 3 UNIVERSITY OF HYDERABAD CAMPUS SCHOOL ……………………………………………………………………………………………………… UH/UHCS/Admn-2026-27/359 Date: 06.12.2025. Admission Notification for LKG for the academic year 2026-2027 Admissions are open for 50 seats in class LKG, with a strength of 25 in each section, for the academic session 2026-2027. Please carry the original birth certificate of the child to collect the challan from the school office. The application fee is Rs. 200/- for SC/ST and Rs.400/- for others has to paid at SBI, HCU branch. Please collect the application by handing over counterfoil of the fee paid. Candidates belonging to SC/ST should carry the latest original caste certificate to avail concession of application fee. Admission process will be as per the admission guidelines and as per the schedule given below. Admission Schedule Note: No correspondence will be entertained once the admissions are closed. S.No Process Date 1. Issue of application forms 15.12.2025 (Monday) to 24.01.2026 (Saturday) on all working days between 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. 2. Last date for submission of filled in application forms. 24.01.2026 (Saturday) by 3:00 p.m. 3. Interactive Session for Category- I 07.02.2026 (Saturday) 9:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. 4. Provisional List of Category I & Completion of formalities. 11.02.2026 (Wednesday) 5. Final List of Category I 16.02.2026 (Monday) 6. Draw of Lots for Category II & III 27.02.2026 (Friday) at 11.00 a.m. 7. Interactive Session for candidates selected in the lottery. 28.02.2026 (Saturday)9:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. 8. Provisional List of Category II & III 13.03.2026 (Friday) 9. Final List of Category II & III 24.03.2026 (Tuesday) 10. Close of Admissions 31.03.2026 (Tuesday) Page 2 of 3 • “A draw of lots shall be taken for the categories, where the number of applicants exceeds the available seats in that particular category” Please carry all the supporting original certificates of your claim along with a copy of the original certificates and duly filled-in application. Original certificates are to be shown and collect them back along with the acknowledgement on successful submission of the application form. You may require the following documents: 1. Birth certificate. 2. Community/Caste certificate in case of SC/ST/OBC (Non-Creamy Layer) (OBC certificate issued by the Competent Authority will only be considered) 3. Proof of Residence. 4. Proof of eligibility for category I, II & University of Hyderabad pensioners. 5. Aadhaar card of Child, Mother and Father. Please note that, extension of time will not be given for producing any document, under any circumstances, the application for admission will not be accepted with insufficient documentation. Note:- It is mandatory that the name recorded on the Aadhaar card and the Date of Birth certificate must be identical. Criteria for Admission Age: As per NEP 2020, the entry age to seek admission into L.K.G is four years plus and less than five years as on 31st March, the year in which the student is seeking admission. Admission is open to only those candidates born on or after 31.3.2021 and on or before 31.03.2022. The candidates picked up in the lottery shall be called for an interactive session, with the panel of teachers, to ascertain the minimum requisite skills-Mental ability, Psychomotor skills etc. Mere calling for the interactive session will not confer any right to claim admission. Priority Categories The following priorities shall be considered for admission, in the order mentioned below. CATEGORY I 1 – Children of permanent employees and the employees on deputation at the University of Hyderabad. Page 3 of 3 Once Category I students are admitted, for the remaining vacancies the following priorities shall be followed in granting admissions. CATEGORY II II A – Children of students of the University of Hyderabad that includes Research Scholars, post-Doctoral Fellows and other Bonafide students, followed by children of project staff and then outsourced /contractual staff of the University of Hyderabad-The outsourced /contractual staff seeking admission shall have completed at least 3 years of service as outsourced /contractual staff in the University as on the last date of submission of application for admission. II B – Grandchildren of permanent and retired employees of the University of Hyderabad- Each of the categories – permanent and retired (employees) shall be allotted 50% of the available vacancies. The allotment is interchangeable within II B in case of shortage of applicants in a given category i.e permanent/ retired. II C – Children of alumni of the University of Hyderabad Campus School, not exceeding three admissions in a given academic year. Out of the available seats, if any, after admitting Category I and Category II, following priorities shall be followed in granting admission. CATEGORY III 50% shall be reserved for Children of transferable and non-transferable employees of Autonomous Bodies/public sector Undertaking/Institute of Higher Learning of the Government of India that are serving/ in collaboration with/have a tie-up with the University of Hyderabad. No application shall be considered under two different categories. Note: 1. Please visit the website www.uohyd.ac.in for detailed admission guidelines and latest updates. 2. Incomplete applications and applications submitted/received after the last date will be rejected. No correspondence in this regard will be entertained. 3. In all admission related matters, the decision of SMC is final and binding on every body. 4. The school reserves the right to cancel/modify/amend the notification as deemed fit. Sd/- Principal
